EC759EB0DFE5013106F068A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate conversational, general academic, and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal spatial and temporal relationships (e.g., After dinner that night we went looking for them).

EC7552E0DFE5013106EF68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish shades of meaning among related words that describe states of mind or degrees of certainty (e.g., knew, believed, suspected, heard, wondered).

EC750210DFE5013106EE68A86D17958E.description: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., describe people who are friendly or helpful).

EC74AC00DFE5013106ED68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish the literal and nonliteral meanings of words and phrases in context (e.g., take steps).

EC744990DFE5013106EC68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.

EC73EFE0DFE5013106EB68A86D17958E.description: Use glossaries or beginning dictionaries, both print and digital, to determine or clarify the precise meaning of key words and phrases.

EC73A140DFE5013106EA68A86D17958E.description: Use a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word with the same root (e.g., company, companion).

EC7352D0DFE5013106E968A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known affix is added to a known word (e.g., agreeable/disagreeable, comfortable/uncomfortable, care/careless, heat/preheat).

EC7305C0DFE5013106E868A86D17958E.description: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

EC721300DFE5013106E568A86D17958E.description: Recognize and observe differences between the conventions of spoken and written standard English.

EC71C760DFE5013106E468A86D17958E.description: Choose words and phrases for effect.

EC717E60DFE5013106E368A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

EC7098C0DFE5013106E068A86D17958E.description: Use spelling patterns and generalizations (e.g., word families, position-based spellings, syllable patterns, ending rules, meaningful word parts) in writing words.

EC6B80F0DFE5013106D068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

EC6A76D0DFE5013106CD68A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when encountering an unknown term important to comprehension or expression.

F9875A40DFE501311FB168A86D17958E.description: Students make informed verbal and written observations about the arts by developing skills for critical analysis through the study of and exposure to the arts.

comments: Critical analysis is the process of inquiry associated with an individual's knowledge of the arts. Communication about the arts in a structured way provides the individual with means to describe, analyze, interpret, and make critical, reasoned judgments about the form and content of the arts.

F984CAC0DFE501311FA968A86D17958E.description: Students develop historical and cultural perspective by recognizing and understanding that the arts throughout history are a record of human experience with a past, present, and future.

comments: Historical and cultural perspective is the vehicle for understanding works of art in time and place. The arts survive through times of interruption and neglect; they outlive governments, creeds, societies, and even the civilizations that spawned them. The artist is a harbinger of change, a translator of social thought, an analyst of cultures, a poetic scientist, and a recorder of history. To understand creative output in the history of the arts is to understand history itself.

F9823370DFE501311FA168A86D17958E.description: Students develop aesthetic perception through the knowledge of art forms and respect for their commonalities and differences.

comments: The study of aesthetics, or the philosophy of the arts, cultivates the direct experience of the senses and supplies the individual with a structure for perceiving and responding to the arts. A grasp of aesthetics empowers the individual to experience beauty in many forms, to appreciate artistic expression, and to develop insight into the creations and performances of others. By questioning concepts, weighing evidence, and examining intuitive reactions, the individual becomes increasingly discriminating in formulating preferences and conclusions about the values inherent in art. Aesthetic perception promotes creativity, flexible thinking, and the pursuit of excellence.

comments: Modeling is best interpreted not as a collection of isolated topics but in relation to other standards. Making mathematical models is a Standard for Mathematical Practice, and specific modeling standards appear throughout the high school standards indicated by a star symbol (★). The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

EA626010DFE5013102E968A86D17958E.description: Explain why the sum or product of two rational numbers is rational; that the sum of a rational number and an irrational number is irrational; and that the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is irrational.

EA620B60DFE5013102E868A86D17958E.description: Use properties of rational and irrational numbers.

EA614D90DFE5013102E668A86D17958E.description: Explain how the definition of the meaning of rational exponents follows from extending the properties of integer exponents to those values, allowing for a notation for radicals in terms of rational exponents.
comments: For example, we define 5<sup>1/3</sup> to be the cube root of 5 because we want (5<sup>1/3</sup>)³ = 5(<sup>1/3</sup>)³ to hold, so (5<sup>1/3</sup>)³ must equal 5.

EA60F770DFE5013102E568A86D17958E.description: Extend the properties of exponents to rational exponents.

B3C6388815A7429E881C461637F4066A.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

4518A7FF3E6C4261BE17C0C8B57F1986.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

959F28CFA29A436F8D0D394287500A58.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

E0A0E959493A4F46B317A5792A723315.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Louisiana Student Standards for English Language Arts and Literacy

ECC41A30DFE50131079368A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal precise actions, emotions, or states of being (e.g., quizzed, whined, stammered) and that are basic to a particular topic (e.g., wildlife, conservation, and endangered when discussing animal preservation).

ECC3B840DFE50131079268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of words by relating them to their opposites (antonyms) and to words with similar but not identical meanings (synonyms).

ECC36290DFE50131079168A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.

ECC301E0DFE50131079068A86D17958E.description: Explain the meaning of simple similes and metaphors (e.g., as pretty as a picture) in context.

ECC2B700DFE50131078F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

ECC26320DFE50131078E68A86D17958E.description: Consult reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation and determine or clarify the precise meaning of key words and phrases.

ECC1F810DFE50131078D68A86D17958E.description: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek and Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., telegraph, photograph, autograph).

ECC193B0DFE50131078C68A86D17958E.description: Use context (e.g., definitions, examples, or restatements in text) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

ECC144D0DFE50131078B68A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 4 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.

ECC0A8D0DFE50131078968A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between contexts that call for formal English (e.g., presenting ideas) and situations where informal discourse is appropriate (e.g., small-group discussion).

ECC00290DFE50131078768A86D17958E.description: Choose words and phrases to convey ideas precisely.

ECBFB600DFE50131078668A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

ECBF1CC0DFE50131078468A86D17958E.description: Spell grade-appropriate words correctly, consulting references as needed.

ECBEC5D0DFE50131078368A86D17958E.description: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence.

ECBE66D0DFE50131078268A86D17958E.description: Use commas and quotation marks to mark direct speech and quotations from a text.

ECBDBAA0DFE50131078068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

ECBD6B60DFE50131077F68A86D17958E.description: Correctly use frequently confused words (e.g., to, too, two; there, their).

ECBD1790DFE50131077E68A86D17958E.description: Produce complete sentences, recognizing and correcting inappropriate fragments and run-ons.

ECBC7460DFE50131077C68A86D17958E.description: Order adjectives within sentences according to conventional patterns (e.g., a small red bag rather than a red small bag).

ECBC16F0DFE50131077B68A86D17958E.description: Use modal auxiliaries (e.g., can, may, must) to convey various conditions.

ECBBC990DFE50131077A68A86D17958E.description: Form and use the progressive (e.g., I was walking; I am walking; I will be walking) verb tenses.

ECBB6DC0DFE50131077968A86D17958E.description: Use relative pronouns (who, whose, whom, which, that) and relative adverbs (where, when, why).

ECBB1A10DFE50131077868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

ECBA3500DFE50131077568A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when encountering an unknown term important to comprehension or expression.

ECB9D8A0DFE50131077468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

ECB973E0DFE50131077368A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

ECB8CCE0DFE50131077168A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

ECB83070DFE50131076F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

ECB7CEA0DFE50131076E68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

ECB148D0DFE50131075A68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

ECB0D160DFE50131075968A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

ECB07350DFE50131075868A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

ECAFE300DFE50131075668A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Speaking and Listening

ECAF9970DFE50131075568A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.

ECAEAC40DFE50131075268A86D17958E.description: Apply grade 4 Reading standards to literature (e.g., "Describe in depth a character, setting, or event in a story or drama, drawing on specific details in the text [e.g., a character's thoughts, words, or actions].").

ECAE1100DFE50131075068A86D17958E.description: Recall relevant information from experiences or gather relevant information from print and digital sources; take notes and categorize information, and provide a list of sources.

ECADC0F0DFE50131074F68A86D17958E.description: Conduct short research projects that build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.

ECAD0780DFE50131074D68A86D17958E.description: With some guidance and support from adults, use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing as well as to interact and collaborate with others; demonstrate sufficient command of keyboarding skills to type a minimum of one page in a single sitting.

ECABA080DFE50131074968A86D17958E.description: Provide a conclusion that follows from the narrated experiences or events.

ECA48B00DFE50131073468A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

ECA3EAC0DFE50131073268A86D17958E.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

E6FB3980DFE50131FD5068A86D17958E.description: In learning environmental science, students will develop an appreciation of the natural environment, learn the importance of environmental quality, and acquire a sense of stewardship. As consumers and citizens, they will be able to recognize how our personal, professional, and political actions affect the natural world.

comments: Environmental education is a process aimed at the development of a literate citizenry which is aware of and shows concern for the total environment and its associated problems. This goal will be met by developing the knowledge, attitudes, motivation, commitment, and skills to work individually and collectively toward the solutions of current problems and the prevention of new ones.

E6F1D0E0DFE50131FD3368A86D17958E.description: The students will develop an understanding of the properties of earth materials, the structure of the earth system, the earth's history, and the earth's place in the universe.

comments: In order to develop a basic understanding of our world, it is essential for students to reflect upon the structure, order, and origin of the universe. This understanding occurs gradually over time as students observe, investigate, model, describe, and find patterns in a changing world. As humans modify their surroundings, they must reflect upon the consequences that these changes will bring. Scientific knowledge about environmental forces and resources will provide a rich topic for critical thinking by students to analyze the effects of their choices on the world.

E99F3C20DFE50131019A68A86D17958E.description: Use the four operations with whole numbers to solve problems.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
E99EA420DFE50131019868A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

E99E5300DFE50131019768A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

E99CEEA0DFE50131019368A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

E99C4020DFE50131019168A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

EA5FDA00DFE5013102E268A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
EA5F5410DFE5013102E168A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
EA5D9B90DFE5013102DD68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

EA5CBFE0DFE5013102DB68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

EE64DDA0DFE501310AA068A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

EE648D80DFE501310A9F68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish among the connotations (associations) of words with similar denotations (definitions) (e.g., bullheaded, willful, firm, persistent, resolute).

EE643EA0DFE501310A9E68A86D17958E.description: Use the relationship between particular words to better understand each of the words.

EE63EEA0DFE501310A9D68A86D17958E.description: Interpret figures of speech (e.g. verbal irony, puns) in context.

EE639670DFE501310A9C68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

EE631650DFE501310A9B68A86D17958E.description: Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).

EE62B860DFE501310A9A68A86D17958E.description: Consult general and specialized reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation of a word or determine or clarify its precise meaning or its part of speech.

EE626870DFE501310A9968A86D17958E.description: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., precede, recede, secede).

EE621690DFE501310A9868A86D17958E.description: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word's position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

EE61C500DFE501310A9768A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words or phrases based on grade 8 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.

EE611A60DFE501310A9568A86D17958E.description: Use verbs in the active and passive voice and in the conditional and subjunctive mood to achieve particular effects (e.g., emphasizing the actor or the action; expressing uncertainty or describing a state contrary to fact).

EE60CBB0DFE501310A9468A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

EE5FD470DFE501310A9168A86D17958E.description: Use an ellipsis to indicate an omission.

EE5F28B0DFE501310A8F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

EE5ECEF0DFE501310A8E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in verb voice and mood.

EE5D3BE0DFE501310A8A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

EE5BF6A0DFE501310A8668A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

EE5BAA00DFE501310A8568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

EE5B5D80DFE501310A8468A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

E8E3E620DFE5013100C368A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

E8E38A50DFE5013100C268A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

E8E232F0DFE5013100BE68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

E8E199B0DFE5013100BC68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

BCA2E836BD194EA3BDF6FEAAD19270A9.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

66C56E3B4C964BA89E64321D2929AC9A.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

BA7933AFE6214A39BB243F83B30F98D9.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

997C7A760563433EBB91F494DDE0412A.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Louisiana Student Standards for English Language Arts and Literacy

EC27E5D0DFE50131064968A86D17958E.description: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts, including using adjectives and adverbs to describe (e.g., When other kids are happy that makes me happy).

EC26E680DFE50131064668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.

EC25ACC0DFE50131064268A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known prefix is added to a known word (e.g., happy/unhappy, tell/retell).

EC2538B0DFE50131064168A86D17958E.description: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

EC24EE70DFE50131064068A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 2 reading and content, choosing flexibly from an array of strategies.

EC245B10DFE50131063E68A86D17958E.description: Compare formal and informal uses of English.

EC240F80DFE50131063D68A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

EC2365C0DFE50131063B68A86D17958E.description: Consult reference materials, including beginning dictionaries, as needed to check and correct spellings.

EC231670DFE50131063A68A86D17958E.description: Generalize learned spelling patterns when writing words (e.g., cage → badge; boy → boil).

EC227DB0DFE50131063868A86D17958E.description: Use commas in greetings and closings of letters.

EC2231D0DFE50131063768A86D17958E.description: Capitalize holidays, product names, and geographic names.

EC21E310DFE50131063668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

EC219060DFE50131063568A86D17958E.description: Produce, expand, and rearrange complete simple and compound sentences (e.g., The boy watched the movie; The little boy watched the movie; The action movie was watched by the little boy).

EC214520DFE50131063468A86D17958E.description: Use adjectives and adverbs, and choose between them depending on what is to be modified.

EC20F8B0DFE50131063368A86D17958E.description: Form and use the past tense of frequently occurring irregular verbs (e.g., sat, hid, told).

EC2049C0DFE50131063168A86D17958E.description: Form and use frequently occurring irregular plural nouns (e.g., feet, children, teeth, mice, fish).

EC1F62A0DFE50131062F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

EC1E7510DFE50131062C68A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when encountering an unknown term important to comprehension or expression.

EC1E1F00DFE50131062B68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

EC1DD370DFE50131062A68A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

EC1D38B0DFE50131062868A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

EC1C9D60DFE50131062668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

EC1C4360DFE50131062568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

EC1B9650DFE50131062368A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Language

EC1B37E0DFE50131062268A86D17958E.description: Produce complete sentences when appropriate to task and situation in order to provide requested detail or clarification.

EC1AD960DFE50131062168A86D17958E.description: Create audio recordings of stories or poems; add drawings or other visual displays to stories or recounts of experiences when appropriate to clarify ideas, thoughts, and feelings.

EC1A8230DFE50131062068A86D17958E.description: Tell a story or recount an experience with appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details, speaking audibly in coherent sentences.

EC19D0D0DFE50131061E68A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to clarify comprehension, gather additional information, or deepen understanding of a topic or issue.

EC1975A0DFE50131061D68A86D17958E.description: Recount or describe key ideas or details from a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media.

EC192DC0DFE50131061C68A86D17958E.description: Ask for clarification and further explanation as needed about the topics and texts under discussion.

EC18E350DFE50131061B68A86D17958E.description: Build on others' talk in conversations by linking their comments to the remarks of others.

EC188F90DFE50131061A68A86D17958E.description: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (e.g., gaining the floor in respectful ways, listening to others with care, speaking one at a time about the topics and texts under discussion).

EC184450DFE50131061968A86D17958E.description: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 2 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.

EC176580DFE50131061668A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

EC171360DFE50131061568A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

EC16B710DFE50131061468A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

EC1606F0DFE50131061268A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

EC15B060DFE50131061168A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

EC156180DFE50131061068A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

EC136DB0DFE50131060A68A86D17958E.description: Recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.

EC131150DFE50131060968A86D17958E.description: Participate in shared research and writing projects (e.g., read a number of books on a single topic to produce a report; record science observations).

EC12C890DFE50131060868A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

EC1230B0DFE50131060668A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from adults, use a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.

EC11E380DFE50131060568A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from adults and peers, focus on a topic and strengthen writing as needed by revising and editing.

EC113010DFE50131060368A86D17958E.description: Write narratives in which they recount a well-elaborated event or short sequence of events, include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide a sense of closure.

EC10D480DFE50131060268A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section.

EC107560DFE50131060168A86D17958E.description: Write opinion pieces in which they introduce the topic or book they are writing about, state an opinion, supply reasons that support the opinion, use linking words (e.g., because, and, also) to connect opinion and reasons, and provide a concluding statement or section.

EC0F83D0DFE5013105FE68A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.

EC0EE6F0DFE5013105FC68A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

EC0E9020DFE5013105FB68A86D17958E.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, assess the credibility and accuracy of each source, and integrate the information while avoiding plagiarism.

EC0E4310DFE5013105FA68A86D17958E.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

EC0DF460DFE5013105F968A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

EC0D9EE0DFE5013105F868A86D17958E.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and to interact and collaborate with others.

EC0D5230DFE5013105F768A86D17958E.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.

EC0D04F0DFE5013105F668A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

EC0C53C0DFE5013105F468A86D17958E.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.

EC0BF2C0DFE5013105F368A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

EC0B9DA0DFE5013105F268A86D17958E.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.

EC0AC2A0DFE5013105EF68A86D17958E.description: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.

EC0A6F70DFE5013105EE68A86D17958E.description: Read on-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.

EC0A28F0DFE5013105ED68A86D17958E.description: Read on-level text with purpose and understanding.

EC09E060DFE5013105EC68A86D17958E.description: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.

EC0758E0DFE5013105E468A86D17958E.description: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.

EC03CE60DFE5013105D968A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 2 topic or subject area.

EC031670DFE5013105D768A86D17958E.description: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.

EC02CC50DFE5013105D668A86D17958E.description: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.

EBFF4A80DFE5013105CB68A86D17958E.description: Describe the overall structure of a story, including describing how the beginning introduces the story and the ending concludes the action.

EBFEF400DFE5013105CA68A86D17958E.description: Describe how words and phrases (e.g., regular beats, alliteration, rhymes, repeated lines) supply rhythm and meaning in a story, poem, or song.

EBFE6070DFE5013105C868A86D17958E.description: Describe how characters in a story respond to major events and challenges.

EBFE1310DFE5013105C768A86D17958E.description: Recount stories, including fables and folktales from diverse cultures, and determine their central message, lesson, or moral.

EBFCBE50DFE5013105C368A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

EBFBEA40DFE5013105C068A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.
