document.title: Louisiana Content Standards for Social Studies

F820C9B0DFE501311D8768A86D17958E.description: Discussing the impact of significant contributions made by historic figures from different regions of the world;

F8206C90DFE501311D8668A86D17958E.description: Describing the social and economic impact of major scientific and technological advancements;

F8202330DFE501311D8568A86D17958E.description: Identifying the characteristics and historical development of selected societies throughout the world;

F81F9BB0DFE501311D8368A86D17958E.description: Recognizing how folklore and other cultural elements have contributed to our local, state, and national heritage;

F81F54B0DFE501311D8268A86D17958E.description: Describing the causes and nature of various movements of large groups of people into and within Louisiana and the United States throughout history;

F81F0840DFE501311D8168A86D17958E.description: Identifying the development of democratic principles and discussing how these principles have been exemplified by historic figures, events, and symbols;

F81EB380DFE501311D8068A86D17958E.description: Describing the people, events, and ideas that were significant to the growth and development of our state and nation;

F81E2590DFE501311D7E68A86D17958E.description: Relating the history of the local community and comparing it to other communities of long ago;

F81DDD70DFE501311D7D68A86D17958E.description: Describing and comparing family life in the present and the past;

F81D3D90DFE501311D7B68A86D17958E.description: Identifying and using primary and secondary historical sources to learn about the past;

F81CE560DFE501311D7A68A86D17958E.description: Recognizing that people in different times and places view the world differently;

F81C9E70DFE501311D7968A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating an understanding of the concepts of time and chronology;

F81C0C40DFE501311D7768A86D17958E.description: Students develop a sense of historical perspective as they study the history of their community, state, nation, and world.

comments: History, the written record of the past, examines the forces of change and continuity that have influenced the human experience over time. In our participatory democracy, that knowledge must be shared by all. Americans need to understand the relationship between past and present, the major trends in the historic and contemporary worlds, and key historical turning points. The study of the great sweep of history explains the past so that citizens can understand the present and look toward the future. The standards and benchmarks contained in this strand should be applied throughout the social studies curriculum.

F81B7860DFE501311D7568A86D17958E.description: Identifying the major goods and services produces in the local community and state.

F81B2780DFE501311D7468A86D17958E.description: Explaining why some goods and services are provided by the government through taxing, charging user fees, and borrowing;

F81ACEE0DFE501311D7368A86D17958E.description: Identifying and explaining economic concepts, such as profit as an incentive for people to take economic risk;

F81A5F50DFE501311D7268A86D17958E.description: Explaining how the changes in prices affect incentives to produce, consume, and save;

F81A1280DFE501311D7168A86D17958E.description: Describing how prices are determined by the interactions of buyers and sellers;

F81975D0DFE501311D6F68A86D17958E.description: Explaining and demonstrating why people participate in voluntary exchanges and how money helps in the process;

F8193140DFE501311D6E68A86D17958E.description: Identifying some of the economic institutions, such as households and banks, that make up the economy;

F818EB80DFE501311D6D68A86D17958E.description: Identifying different methods for the distribution of goods and services, including the concept of markets;

F8189B10DFE501311D6C68A86D17958E.description: Determining how the development of skills and knowledge relates to career opportunity and economic well-being;

F8184850DFE501311D6B68A86D17958E.description: Describing how specialization affects productivity and contributes to the need for interdependence among producers and consumers;

F817EF10DFE501311D6A68A86D17958E.description: Describing how natural resources, human resources, and capital (human-made) resources have been used and are combined in the production of goods and services;

F8179890DFE501311D6968A86D17958E.description: Explaining the relationships among producers and consumers;

F8175890DFE501311D6868A86D17958E.description: Discussing and determining the process for making economic decisions;

F8171730DFE501311D6768A86D17958E.description: Demonstrating how economic wants affect decisions about using goods and services;

F816D5C0DFE501311D6668A86D17958E.description: Identifying what is gained and lost when individuals or groups make decisions;

F8168E80DFE501311D6568A86D17958E.description: Recognizing that limited resources require people to make decisions;

F815F0B0DFE501311D6368A86D17958E.description: Students develop an understanding of fundamental economic concepts as they apply to the interdependence and decision making of individuals, households, businesses, and governments in the United States and the world.

comments: Effective economic education in our schools is the key to preparing young people for economic decisions in their personal lives and as citizens in a democratic society. An economically literate work force is critical to the well being of our state and nation. Students need to understand and apply basic economic concepts in order to make reasoned judgments in a complex and changing world. With economic knowledge and decision-making skills, students will be ready to live and work productively in the 21st century. The standards and benchmarks contained in this strand should be applied throughout the social studies curriculum.

F8156660DFE501311D6168A86D17958E.description: Discussing issues related to citizenship and public service.

F8151200DFE501311D6068A86D17958E.description: Describing the many ways that citizens can participate in and contribute to their communities and to American society;

F814A1D0DFE501311D5F68A86D17958E.description: Identifying and discussing civic traits that are important to the preservation and improvement of American constitutional democracy;

F8145660DFE501311D5E68A86D17958E.description: Describing the rights and responsibilities of citizenship in a democratic society;

F8141650DFE501311D5D68A86D17958E.description: Explaining the meaning of citizenship and the means by which individuals become citizens of the United States;

F8139390DFE501311D5B68A86D17958E.description: Explaining that the world is divided into different nations and describing the major ways that these nations interact;

F8130EA0DFE501311D5968A86D17958E.description: Discussing the importance of citizens' sharing and supporting the principles of American constitutional democracy;

F812BF20DFE501311D5868A86D17958E.description: Identifying basic principles of American constitutional democracy and explaining how the constitutions of the United States and Louisiana reflect these principles;

F8127F40DFE501311D5768A86D17958E.description: Foundations of the American political system

F8123F30DFE501311D5668A86D17958E.description: Explaining the purposes and importance of rules and laws;

F811FDE0DFE501311D5568A86D17958E.description: Explaining how officials in government acquire the authority to exercise political power;

F811BDD0DFE501311D5468A86D17958E.description: Identifying key members of government at the local, state, and national levels and describing their powers and the limits on their powers;

F8117C60DFE501311D5368A86D17958E.description: Identifying and describing some of the major responsibilities of local, state, and national governments;

F8113850DFE501311D5268A86D17958E.description: Comparing limited governments to unlimited governments;

F810EAF0DFE501311D5168A86D17958E.description: Explaining the necessity and basic purposes of government;

F8109C80DFE501311D5068A86D17958E.description: Describing government in terms of the people and groups who make, apply, and enforce rules and laws in the home, school, community, and nation;

F8100570DFE501311D4E68A86D17958E.description: Students develop an understanding of the structure and purposes of government, the foundations of the American democratic system, and the role of the United States in the world, while learning about the rights and responsibilities of citizenship.

comments: In order for citizens to exercise their rights and fulfill their responsibilities as members of a self-governing society, they must acquire the knowledge and skills necessary for informed, responsible participation in political life. A commitment to the fundamental principles of American constitutional democracy is essential to its preservation and progression. Because a democratic society must rely on the knowledge, skills, and virtues of its citizens, the study of civics is central to the purpose of American education. The standards and benchmarks contained in this strand should be applied throughout the social studies curriculum.

comments: Geography, the study of the spatial aspects of human existence, enables students to find answers to questions about the world around them. A geographically informed person sees, understands, and appreciates the connections among people, places, and environments. Understanding these connections requires an acute awareness of space, which can be identified in terms of location, distance, direction, pattern, shape, and arrangement. With a strong grasp of geography, students will be prepared to understand issues and solve problems in the contemporary world. The standards and benchmarks contained in this strand should be applied throughout the social studies curriculum.

E73A6050DFE50131FDDA68A86D17958E.description: In learning environmental science, students will develop an appreciation of the natural environment, learn the importance of environmental quality, and acquire a sense of stewardship. comments: Environmental education is a process aimed at the development of a literate citizenry which is aware of and shows concern for the total environment and its associated problems. comments: Function notation is not required in Grade 8.

For example, collect data from students in your class on whether or not they have a curfew on school nights and whether or not they have assigned chores at home. Is there evidence that those who have a curfew also tend to have chores?

EA43E240DFE5013102C268A86D17958E.description: Use similar triangles to explain why the slope m is the same between any two distinct points on a non-vertical line in the coordinate plane; derive the equation y = mx for a line through the origin and the equation y = mx + b for a line intercepting the vertical axis at b.

EA439CE0DFE5013102C168A86D17958E.description: Graph proportional relationships, interpreting the unit rate as the slope of the graph. Compare two different proportional relationships represented in different ways.
comments: For example, compare a distance-time graph to a distance-time equation to determine which of two moving objects has greater speed.

EA4358E0DFE5013102C068A86D17958E.description: Understand the connections between proportional relationships, lines, and linear equations.

EA430D90DFE5013102BF68A86D17958E.description: Perform operations with numbers expressed in scientific notation, including problems where both decimal and scientific notation are used. Use scientific notation and choose units of appropriate size for measurements of very large or very small quantities (e.g., use millimeters per year for seafloor spreading). Interpret scientific notation that has been generated by technology.

comments: For example, estimate the population of the United States as 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> and the population of the world as 7 × 10<sup>9</sup>, and determine that the world population is more than 20 times larger.
EA42BE30DFE5013102BE68A86D17958E.description: Use numbers expressed in the form of a single digit times an integer power of 10 to estimate very large or very small quantities, and to express how many times as much one is than the other.

EA427BB0DFE5013102BD68A86D17958E.description: Use square root and cube root symbols to represent solutions to equations of the form x² = p and x³ = p, where p is a positive rational number. Evaluate square roots of small perfect squares and cube roots of small perfect cubes. Know that √2 is irrational.

EA423780DFE5013102BC68A86D17958E.description: Know and apply the properties of integer exponents to generate equivalent numerical expressions.

EA41F560DFE5013102BB68A86D17958E.description: Work with radicals and integer exponents.

EA416DE0DFE5013102B968A86D17958E.description: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare the size of irrational numbers, locate them approximately on a number line diagram, and estimate the value of expressions (e.g., π²).
comments: For example, by truncating the decimal expansion of √2, show that √2 is between 1 and 2, then between 1.4 and 1.5, and explain how to continue on to get better approximations.

EA4119D0DFE5013102B868A86D17958E.description: Know that numbers that are not rational are called irrational. Understand informally that every number has a decimal expansion; for rational numbers show that the decimal expansion repeats eventually, and convert a decimal expansion which repeats eventually into a rational number.

EA40CB60DFE5013102B768A86D17958E.description: Know that there are numbers that are not rational, and approximate them by rational numbers.

EA4031A0DFE5013102B568A86D17958E.description: Know the formulas for the volumes of cones, cylinders, and spheres and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

EA3FEFC0DFE5013102B468A86D17958E.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving volume of cylinders, cones, and spheres.

EA3FA1C0DFE5013102B368A86D17958E.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points in a coordinate system.

EA3F4C60DFE5013102B268A86D17958E.description: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions.

EA3F0660DFE5013102B168A86D17958E.description: Explain a proof of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.

EA3EC450DFE5013102B068A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply the Pythagorean Theorem.

comments: For example, arrange three copies of the same triangle so that the sum of the three angles appears to form a line, and give an argument in terms of transversals why this is so.
EA3E8330DFE5013102AF68A86D17958E.description: Use informal arguments to establish facts about the angle sum and exterior angle of triangles, about the angles created when parallel lines are cut by a transversal, and the angle-angle criterion for similarity of triangles.

EA3E4090DFE5013102AE68A86D17958E.description: Understand that a two-dimensional figure is similar to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, translations, and dilations; given two similar two-dimensional figures, describe a sequence that exhibits the similarity between them.

EA3DF910DFE5013102AD68A86D17958E.description: Describe the effect of dilations, translations, rotations, and reflections on two-dimensional figures using coordinates.

EA3DACD0DFE5013102AC68A86D17958E.description: Understand that a two-dimensional figure is congruent to another if the second can be obtained from the first by a sequence of rotations, reflections, and translations; given two congruent figures, describe a sequence that exhibits the congruence between them.

EA3D6AB0DFE5013102AB68A86D17958E.description: Parallel lines are taken to parallel lines.

EA3D2800DFE5013102AA68A86D17958E.description: Angles are taken to angles of the same measure.

EA3CE370DFE5013102A968A86D17958E.description: Lines are taken to lines, and line segments to line segments of the same length.

EA3C9C70DFE5013102A868A86D17958E.description: Verify experimentally the properties of rotations, reflections, and translations:

EA3C5110DFE5013102A768A86D17958E.description: Understand congruence and similarity using physical models, transparencies, or geometry software.

EA3BB040DFE5013102A568A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
EA3B5A40DFE5013102A468A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
EA39FF70DFE5013102A068A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
EA394870DFE50131029E68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: Louisiana Content Standards for Social Studies

F90E95A0DFE501311EB468A86D17958E.description: Explaining the worldwide significance of major political, economic, social, cultural, and technological developments and trends;

F90E51B0DFE501311EB368A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the international power shifts and the breakup of colonial empires that occurred in the years following World War II;

F90E0830DFE501311EB268A86D17958E.description: Era 9: The 20th Century Since 1945 (1945 to the Present)

F90DBD90DFE501311EB168A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the causes and international consequences of World War I, the rise and actions of totalitarian systems, World War II, and other early 20th century conflicts;

F90D7290DFE501311EB068A86D17958E.description: Era 8: A Half-Century of Crisis and Achievement (1900-1945)

F90D18E0DFE501311EAF68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the patterns of worldwide change that emerged during the era of Western military and economic domination;

F90CA390DFE501311EAE68A86D17958E.description: Evaluating the economic, political, and social consequences of the agricultural and industrial revolutions on world societies;

F90C4F90DFE501311EAD68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the impact that political revolutions and new ideologies had on societies around the world;

F90BBDF0DFE501311EAB68A86D17958E.description: Tracing the expansion of European power and economic influence in the world and examining the impact of this expansion on societies in Asia and the Americas;

F90B71C0DFE501311EAA68A86D17958E.description: Explaining how the emergence of territorial empires in Europe, Asia, and Africa unified large areas politically, economically, and culturally;

F90B1F80DFE501311EA968A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the political, cultural, and economic developments and trends that resulted in the transformation of major world regions;

F90ACCC0DFE501311EA868A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the impact of transoceanic linking of all major regions of the world;

F90A8230DFE501311EA768A86D17958E.description: Era 6: Emergence of the First Global Age (1450-1770)

F90A39D0DFE501311EA668A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the consequences of the economic and cultural interchange that increasingly developed among the peoples of Europe, Asia, and Africa;

F909AA70DFE501311EA468A86D17958E.description: Summarizing the developments and contributions of civilizations that flourished in Europe, Asia, Africa, and the Americas;

F9095EA0DFE501311EA368A86D17958E.description: Era 4: Expanding Zones of Exchange and Encounter (A.D. 300-1000)

F9090910DFE501311EA268A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the origins, central ideas, and worldwide impact of major religious and philosophical traditions;

F908C240DFE501311EA168A86D17958E.description: Era 3: Classical Traditions, Major Religions, and Giant Empires (1000 B.C.-A.D. 300)

F9087AF0DFE501311EA068A86D17958E.description: Making generalizations about the cultural legacies of both the ancient river and the classical civilizations;

F90830C0DFE501311E9F68A86D17958E.description: Era 2: The Rise of Early Civilization (4000-1000 B.C.)

F907D550DFE501311E9E68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the development of early human communities and civilizations;

F90693C0DFE501311E9B68A86D17958E.description: Discussing and demonstrating an understanding of recent developments in foreign and domestic policies;

F9064650DFE501311E9A68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing developments and issues in contemporary American society;

F905F630DFE501311E9968A86D17958E.description: Explaining the major changes that have resulted as the United States has moved from an industrial to an information society;

F905AAB0DFE501311E9868A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the economic, political, social, and cultural transformation of the United States since World War II;

F9055420DFE501311E9768A86D17958E.description: Examining and summarizing key developments and issues in foreign and domestic policies during the Cold War era;

F9050E00DFE501311E9668A86D17958E.description: Era 9: Contemporary United States (1945 to the Present)

F904C890DFE501311E9568A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the origins, course, and results of World War II;

F90481D0DFE501311E9468A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the causes, developments, and effects of the Great Depression and the New Deal;

F9043A00DFE501311E9368A86D17958E.description: Era 8: The Great Depression and World War II (1929-1945)

F903EC10DFE501311E9268A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the significant changes that evolved in the United States between World War I and the Great Depression;

F9039290DFE501311E9168A86D17958E.description: Explaining the changing role of the United States in world affairs through World War I;

F9034830DFE501311E9068A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the rise of the labor and agrarian movements;

F902EBC0DFE501311E8F68A86D17958E.description: Evaluating the significance of the Progressive Movement;

F9028AB0DFE501311E8E68A86D17958E.description: Era 7: The Emergence of Modern America (1890-1930)

F9023110DFE501311E8D68A86D17958E.description: Describing the immigration and internal migration patterns that have occurred in the history of the United States and examining the cultural and social changes that have resulted;

F901D590DFE501311E8C68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the development of industrialization and examining its impact on American society;

F9018900DFE501311E8B68A86D17958E.description: Era 6: The Development of the Industrial United States (1870-1900)

F90137B0DFE501311E8A68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the origins, major events, and effects of the Civil War and Reconstruction;

F900A3F0DFE501311E8868A86D17958E.description: Tracing territorial expansion and reform movements in the United States;

F8FFEED0DFE501311E8668A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the development of the American constitutional system;

F8FFA770DFE501311E8568A86D17958E.description: Era 3: Revolution and the New Nation (1754-1820s)

F8FF5F70DFE501311E8468A86D17958E.description: Summarizing the process by which the United States was colonized and later became an independent nation;

F8FEC880DFE501311E8268A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the significant changes that resulted from interactions among the peoples of Europe, Africa, and the Americas;

F8FD8140DFE501311E7E68A86D17958E.description: Conducting research in efforts to analyze historical questions and issues;

F8FD2CE0DFE501311E7D68A86D17958E.description: Utilizing knowledge of facts and concepts drawn from history and methods of historical inquiry to analyze historical and contemporary issues;

F8FCE600DFE501311E7C68A86D17958E.description: Interpreting and evaluating the historical evidence presented in primary and secondary sources;

F8FC9AB0DFE501311E7B68A86D17958E.description: Explaining and analyzing events, ideas, and issues within a historical context;

F8FC45F0DFE501311E7A68A86D17958E.description: Applying key concepts, such as chronology and conflict, to explain and analyze patterns of historical change and continuity;

F8FBAEB0DFE501311E7868A86D17958E.description: Students develop a sense of historical perspective as they study the history of their community, state, nation, and world.

comments: History, the written record of the past, examines the forces of change and continuity that have influenced the human experience over time. In our participatory democracy, that knowledge must be shared by all. Americans need to understand the relationship between past and present, the major trends in the historic and contemporary worlds, and key historical turning points. The study of the great sweep of history explains the past so that citizens can understand the present and look toward the future. The standards and benchmarks contained in this strand should be applied throughout the social studies curriculum.

F8FB0500DFE501311E7668A86D17958E.description: Explaining the basic concepts of United States fiscal policy, monetary policy, and regulations and describing their effects on the economy;

F8FAB550DFE501311E7568A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the causes and consequences of unemployment, underemployment, and income distribution in a market economy;

F8FA6760DFE501311E7468A86D17958E.description: Explaining how interest rates, investments, and inflation/deflation impact the economy;

F8FA2300DFE501311E7368A86D17958E.description: Explaining the meanings of such economic indicators as GDP, per capita GDP, real GDP, CPI, and unemployment rate;

F8F99890DFE501311E7168A86D17958E.description: Analyzing Louisiana's role in the national and world economies;

F8F950A0DFE501311E7068A86D17958E.description: Evaluating the effects of domestic policies on international trade;

F8F90120DFE501311E6F68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the causes and consequences of worldwide economic interdependence;

F8F8A230DFE501311E6E68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the impact of governmental taxation, spending, and regulation on different groups in a market economy;

F8F85120DFE501311E6D68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing how changes in supply and demand, price, incentives, and profit influence production and distribution in a competitive market system;

F8F7FE60DFE501311E6C68A86D17958E.description: Identifying factors that cause changes in supply and demand;

F8F772B0DFE501311E6A68A86D17958E.description: Applying economic concepts to understand and evaluate historical and contemporary issues;

F8F72940DFE501311E6968A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the roles of money and banking in an economic system;

F8F6D5F0DFE501311E6868A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the roles of economic institutions, such as corporations and labor unions, that compose economic systems;

F8F68F70DFE501311E6768A86D17958E.description: Explaining the basic features of market structures and exchanges;

F8F5D550DFE501311E6568A86D17958E.description: Applying the skills and knowledge necessary in making decisions about career options;

F8F57F60DFE501311E6468A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the roles that production, distribution, and consumption play in economic decisions;

F8F53870DFE501311E6368A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the impact of the scarcity of productive resources and examining the choices and opportunity cost that result;

F8F49B80DFE501311E6168A86D17958E.description: Students develop an understanding of fundamental economic concepts as they apply to the interdependence and decision making of individuals, households, businesses, and governments in the United States and the world.

comments: Effective economic education in our schools is the key to preparing young people for economic decisions in their personal lives and as citizens in a democratic society. An economically literate work force is critical to the well being of our state and nation. Students need to understand and apply basic economic concepts in order to make reasoned judgments in a complex and changing world. With economic knowledge and decision-making skills, students will be ready to live and work productively in the 21st century. The standards and benchmarks contained in this strand should be applied throughout the social studies curriculum.

F8F405C0DFE501311E5F68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing and evaluating the importance of political leadership, public service, and a knowledgeable citizenry to American constitutional democracy;

F8F3A940DFE501311E5E68A86D17958E.description: Explaining and evaluating the various forms of political participation that citizens can use to monitor and shape the formation and implementation of public policy;

F8F34280DFE501311E5D68A86D17958E.description: Evaluating and defending positions regarding the personal and civic responsibilities and citizens in American constitutional democracy;

F8F2CC40DFE501311E5C68A86D17958E.description: Evaluating and defending positions on issues regarding the personal, political, and economics rights of citizens;

F8F24440DFE501311E5A68A86D17958E.description: Evaluating the impact of American ideas and actions on the world and analyzing the effects of significant international developments on the United States;

F8F1FF30DFE501311E5968A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the major foreign policy positions of the United States and evaluating their consequences;

F8F1B8E0DFE501311E5868A86D17958E.description: Analyzing how the world is organized politically and evaluating how the interaction of political entities, such as nation-states and international organizations, affects the United States;

F8F122A0DFE501311E5668A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the historical and contemporary roles of associations and groups in local, state, and national politics;

F8F0CB90DFE501311E5568A86D17958E.description: Evaluating the roles of political parties, campaigns, and elections in American politics;

F8F07C50DFE501311E5468A86D17958E.description: Evaluating issues related to the differences between American ideals and the realities of American social and political life;

F8F022A0DFE501311E5368A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the nature of American political and social conflict;

F8EFD960DFE501311E5268A86D17958E.description: Explaining basic democratic beliefs and principles of constitutional democracy in American society and applying them to the analysis of issues of conflicting beliefs and principles;

F8EF9070DFE501311E5168A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the central ideas and historical origins of American constitutional government and evaluating how this form of government has helped to shaped American society;

F8EF4080DFE501311E5068A86D17958E.description: Foundations of the American political system

F8EEED00DFE501311E4F68A86D17958E.description: Explaining how government is financed through taxation;

F8EEA5A0DFE501311E4E68A86D17958E.description: Examining the major responsibilities of the national government for domestic and foreign policy;

F8EE5D20DFE501311E4D68A86D17958E.description: Evaluating the role and importance of law in the American political system and applying criteria to evaluate laws;

F8EE14E0DFE501311E4C68A86D17958E.description: Explaining the organization and functions of local, state, and national governments and evaluating their relationships;

F8EDC8E0DFE501311E4B68A86D17958E.description: Explaining and evaluating issues related to the distribution of powers and responsibilities within the federal system;

F8ED7A20DFE501311E4A68A86D17958E.description: Comparing and evaluating the essential characteristics of various systems of government and identifying historical and contemporary examples of each;

F8ED2530DFE501311E4968A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the necessity and purposes of politics and government and identifying examples of programs that fit within those purposes;

F8EC94F0DFE501311E4768A86D17958E.description: Students develop an understanding of the structure and purposes of government, the foundations of the American democratic system, and the role of the United States in the world, while learning about the rights and responsibilities of citizenship.

comments: In order for citizens to exercise their rights and fulfill their responsibilities as members of a self-governing society, they must acquire the knowledge and skills necessary for informed, responsible participation in political life. A commitment to the fundamental principles of American constitutional democracy is essential to its preservation and progression. Because a democratic society must rely on the knowledge, skills, and virtues of its citizens, the study of civics is central to the purpose of American education. The standards and benchmarks contained in this strand should be applied throughout the social studies curriculum.

F8EBEF30DFE501311E4568A86D17958E.description: Developing plans to solve local and regional geographic problems related to contemporary issues.

F8EB91C0DFE501311E4468A86D17958E.description: Evaluating policies and programs related to the use of natural resources;

F8EB3630DFE501311E4368A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the relationship between natural resources and the exploration, colonization, settlement, and uses of land in different regions of the world;

F8EAE550DFE501311E4268A86D17958E.description: Examining the challenges placed on human systems by the physical environment and formulating strategies to deal with these challenges;

F8EA8EE0DFE501311E4168A86D17958E.description: Describing and evaluating the ways in which technology has expanded the human capability to modify the physical environment;

F8E9E220DFE501311E3F68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing how cooperation, conflict, and self-interests impact social, political, and economic entities on Earth;

F8E989E0DFE501311E3E68A86D17958E.description: Describing and evaluating spatial distributions of economics systems and how economic systems affect regions;

F8E93A50DFE501311E3D68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing the characteristics, distribution, and interrelationships of the world's cultures;

F8E8F0B0DFE501311E3C68A86D17958E.description: Analyzing trends in world population numbers and patterns and predicting their consequences;

E9797970DFE50131015968A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

E9792A50DFE50131015868A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

E977D8E0DFE50131015468A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

E976E9F0DFE50131015268A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Louisiana Student Standards for English Language Arts and Literacy

EDFFB400DFE5013109D168A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.

EDFF1BB0DFE5013109CF68A86D17958E.description: Use the relationship between particular words (e.g., synonym/antonym, analogy) to better understand each of the words.

EDFE7250DFE5013109CD68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

EDFE15C0DFE5013109CC68A86D17958E.description: Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).

EDFDBFF0DFE5013109CB68A86D17958E.description: Consult general and specialized reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation of a word or determine or clarify its precise meaning or its part of speech.

E905A700DFE5013100F468A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

E90559B0DFE5013100F368A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

E9040520DFE5013100EF68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

E9036550DFE5013100ED68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

EDA54BD6237E4C09A5651F024E5DB8A1.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

3C741C6E27CE414AA9894E88CA124D3A.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
14862BB96C9347E7B6E0D893C09E4BC5.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

DF3E1B6FB756459AA7A04F9D8A6858D5.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

E9EBBCA0DFE50131021A68A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

E9EB6B70DFE50131021968A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

E9EA2360DFE50131021568A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

E9E970A0DFE50131021368A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
